subject: history
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: On what date was the armistice ending the First World War signed?
options: 11 November 1918
9 November 1918
28 June 1919
1 August 1914
questions.explain: The armistice was signed on 11 November 1918, ending the fighting of the First World War.

questions.q: Which German leader abdicated in November 1918, allowing the Weimar Republic to be created?
options: Kaiser Wilhelm II
Friedrich Ebert
Paul von Hindenburg
Gustav Stresemann
questions.explain: Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicated on 9 November 1918 and fled to the Netherlands.

questions.q: Why was the 'stab in the back' myth (Dolchstoss) damaging to the new Weimar government?
options: It blamed the politicians who signed the armistice for betraying the army
It claimed the Kaiser had been assassinated by communists
It argued that Germany had actually won the war
It accused the army generals of cowardice
questions.explain: The myth held that the 'November Criminals' had betrayed an undefeated army, undermining trust in the Republic's leaders.

questions.q: Which article of the Treaty of Versailles forced Germany to accept blame for the war?
options: Article 231 (the War Guilt clause)
Article 48
Article 25
Article 80
questions.explain: Article 231, the War Guilt clause, required Germany to accept responsibility for causing the war.

questions.q: What was a major weakness of the Weimar Constitution's use of proportional representation?
options: It produced many small parties, making stable coalition government difficult
It gave the President no powers at all
It banned all political parties except the SPD
It prevented anyone under 30 from voting
questions.explain: Proportional representation split the Reichstag among many parties, so weak, short-lived coalitions were common.

questions.q: What triggered the hyperinflation crisis of 1923?
options: France and Belgium occupied the Ruhr after Germany missed reparations payments
The Wall Street Crash wiped out German savings
Britain refused to trade with Germany
The Kapp Putsch seized the national bank
questions.explain: The Ruhr occupation led the government to print money to pay striking workers, causing hyperinflation.

questions.q: Which new currency did Gustav Stresemann introduce in late 1923 to end hyperinflation?
options: The Rentenmark
The Reichsmark
The Goldmark
The Euro
questions.explain: Stresemann introduced the Rentenmark in November 1923 to restore confidence in Germany's currency.

questions.q: A student argues the years 1924-29 were a 'golden age' for Weimar. Which piece of evidence best supports this?
options: The Dawes Plan and US loans helped German industry and the economy recover
The Nazi Party won the most seats in the Reichstag
Hyperinflation destroyed the savings of the middle class
The Kapp Putsch overthrew the government
questions.explain: The Dawes Plan (1924) brought US loans and reorganised reparations, fuelling economic recovery in this period.

questions.q: Which agreement of 1925 improved Germany's relations with France by accepting its western borders?
options: The Locarno Pact
The Treaty of Rapallo
The Kellogg-Briand Pact
The Young Plan
questions.explain: In the Locarno Pact (1925) Germany accepted its western borders, improving relations and leading to League membership.

questions.q: What was the name of the party that Hitler took over and renamed the NSDAP (Nazi Party)?
options: The German Workers' Party (DAP)
The Social Democratic Party (SPD)
The Communist Party (KPD)
The Centre Party
questions.explain: Hitler joined the German Workers' Party (DAP) in 1919 and it was renamed the NSDAP in 1920.

questions.q: What was the main significance of the Munich (Beer Hall) Putsch of November 1923 for Hitler?
options: Its failure led him to pursue power through legal, electoral means
It made him Chancellor of Germany immediately
It gave the Nazis control of the army
It banned the SPD from politics
questions.explain: The failed putsch convinced Hitler to gain power legally through elections rather than by force.

questions.q: What book did Hitler write while imprisoned in Landsberg after the Munich Putsch?
options: Mein Kampf
The 25 Point Programme
Das Kapital
The Doctrine of Fascism
questions.explain: Hitler wrote Mein Kampf ('My Struggle') in prison, setting out his political and racial ideas.

questions.q: Why did support for the Nazi Party grow rapidly after 1929?
options: The Wall Street Crash caused mass unemployment and economic depression
The Weimar economy was booming and stable
The Treaty of Versailles was cancelled
The Nazis promised to keep the Weimar Constitution unchanged
questions.explain: The Depression created mass unemployment, and desperate voters turned to the Nazis' promises of recovery.

questions.q: What was the role of the SA (Sturmabteilung) in the Nazis' rise?
options: Paramilitary 'brownshirts' who intimidated opponents and protected Nazi meetings
The Nazi women's organisation
The party's finance department
Hitler's personal bodyguard elite unit
questions.explain: The SA were the brownshirted stormtroopers who fought opponents and provided a show of Nazi strength.

questions.q: How did Hitler become Chancellor on 30 January 1933?
options: Hindenburg and von Papen appointed him, believing they could control him
He won an outright majority of seats in a general election
He led a successful armed coup against the government
He was elected President of Germany
questions.explain: Conservative politicians persuaded Hindenburg to appoint Hitler Chancellor, wrongly expecting to control him.

questions.q: What event on 27 February 1933 did Hitler use to arrest communists and increase his power?
options: The Reichstag Fire
The Night of the Long Knives
Kristallnacht
The Munich Putsch
questions.explain: The Reichstag Fire was blamed on communists and used to justify emergency powers and mass arrests.

questions.q: Why was the Enabling Act of March 1933 so important to Hitler's dictatorship?
options: It let him make laws without the Reichstag or the President for four years
It made Hitler President as well as Chancellor
It banned the Nazi Party's rivals from voting
It gave women the right to hold office
questions.explain: The Enabling Act allowed Hitler to pass laws without Reichstag approval, the legal basis of his dictatorship.

questions.q: During the Night of the Long Knives in June 1934, who did Hitler have murdered?
options: Ernst Rohm and leaders of the SA
The entire Reichstag
Members of the Catholic Church
The generals of the German army
questions.explain: Hitler had SA leader Ernst Rohm and other opponents killed to remove threats and win army support.

questions.q: What did Hitler do after President Hindenburg died in August 1934 to complete his control?
options: He combined the roles of Chancellor and President as 'Fuhrer' and made the army swear loyalty to him
He restored the Weimar Constitution
He held free multi-party elections
He handed power to the army generals
questions.explain: On Hindenburg's death Hitler merged both offices as Fuhrer and had the army swear a personal oath to him.

questions.q: A historian studies how the Nazis created a 'police state'. Which organisation best illustrates this?
options: The Gestapo, the secret police who spied on and arrested opponents
The Hitler Youth, which trained boys
The Reich Labour Service, which built roads
The League of German Maidens for girls
questions.explain: The Gestapo were the secret police central to the terror and surveillance of the Nazi police state.

questions.q: What were the two organisations that made up the Nazi youth movement for boys and girls?
options: The Hitler Youth and the League of German Maidens
The SA and the SS
The Gestapo and the Kripo
The Rentenbank and the Reichsbank
questions.explain: Boys joined the Hitler Youth and girls the League of German Maidens (BDM) to be indoctrinated in Nazi ideas.

questions.q: The Nazi slogan 'Kinder, Kuche, Kirche' summed up their view that women should focus on what?
options: Children, cooking and the church (home and family)
Careers, culture and commerce
Combat, command and control
Communism, capitalism and the constitution
questions.explain: Nazi policy encouraged women to leave work and devote themselves to children, home and church.

questions.q: What did the Nuremberg Laws of 1935 do to Jewish people in Germany?
options: Removed their citizenship and banned marriage between Jews and non-Jews
Gave them equal rights with other Germans
Forced them to join the Hitler Youth
Allowed them to hold government jobs
questions.explain: The Nuremberg Laws stripped Jews of German citizenship and outlawed marriage or relations with non-Jews.

questions.q: Why is Kristallnacht (November 1938) seen as a turning point in Nazi persecution of Jews?
options: It was a state-encouraged wave of violence destroying Jewish homes, shops and synagogues
It gave Jews full legal protection
It ended all anti-Jewish laws
It was a peaceful protest organised by Jewish leaders
questions.explain: Kristallnacht saw organised destruction of Jewish property and mass arrests, marking a shift to open violence.

questions.q: A source claims the Nazis reduced unemployment before 1939. Which policy best supports this claim?
options: Public works such as building autobahns and the Reich Labour Service (RAD)
Closing all German factories
Banning men from working
Cutting the size of the army to zero
questions.explain: Schemes like autobahn construction, the RAD and rearmament created jobs and cut official unemployment.
